records.name: Olfactory nerve (CN I)
records.root_values: Arises from the cerebrum — one of the two cranial nerves that do not arise from the brainstem; its fibres are the axons of the olfactory receptor neurons of the nasal epithelium, which project to the olfactory bulb.
records.course: From the olfactory epithelium of the nasal cavity, the nerve fibres pass upward through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to the olfactory bulb.
records.motor_distribution: None — the nerve is purely sensory (special visceral sensory, SVS).
records.sensory_distribution: Smell (special visceral sensory).
records.clinical_testing: Tested by presenting common smells (for example coffee or mint) to one nostril at a time; the patient should be able to recognise the smell. Loss of the sense of smell is anosmia, which can follow blunt head trauma if all the fibres are sheared as the brain moves within the cranium.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Optic nerve (CN II)
records.root_values: Arises from the cerebrum; the nerve carries the axons of the retina — including the photosensitive ganglion cells that send the signal for the pupillary light response — to the brain.
records.course: From the retina, the nerve enters the cranium through the optic canal and meets its fellow at the optic chiasm, where fibres sort so that the two halves of the visual field are processed by opposite sides of the brain.
records.motor_distribution: None — the nerve is purely sensory (special somatic sensory, SSS).
records.sensory_distribution: Vision (special somatic sensory).
records.clinical_testing: Visual acuity is tested with a Snellen chart; the extent of the visual field is tested by establishing the boundaries of peripheral vision; the optic disk, where the optic nerve emerges from the eye, is inspected through the pupil with an ophthalmoscope. The nerve is the afferent (sensory) limb of the pupillary light reflex. Loss of peripheral vision ('tunnel vision') may result from a pituitary tumour pressing on the optic chiasm.
records.note: Links the BodyParts3D 4.0 inventory records named in geometry_record_ids, which carry geometry in the nervous system module (Milestone 9).

records.name: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
records.root_values: Arises at the midbrain–pontine junction of the brainstem.
records.course: From the midbrain–pontine junction, the nerve passes to the orbit and enters it through the superior orbital fissure.
records.motor_distribution: Somatic motor (GSM): four extrinsic eye muscles — superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus and inferior oblique (all the extraocular muscles except lateral rectus and superior oblique) — and the levator palpebrae superioris. Visceral motor (GVM, parasympathetic): the pupillary sphincter, and control of the shape of the lens for accommodation.
records.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve is motor only (general somatic motor and general visceral motor).
records.clinical_testing: Eye movement is tested by having the patient track the tip of a pen through the visual field, watching for conjugate movement; failure of one eye to move in conjugation with the other produces diplopia. Moving the pen in toward the face tests convergence and accommodation. The nerve is the efferent (motor) limb of the pupillary light reflex: if light in either eye elicits constriction in only one eye, the problem is with the oculomotor system.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
records.root_values: Arises from the posterior side of the midbrain; it has the longest intracranial length of all the cranial nerves.
records.course: From the posterior midbrain, the nerve travels to the orbit and enters it through the superior orbital fissure.
records.motor_distribution: The superior oblique muscle (general somatic motor), which rotates the eye along its axis medially (intorsion).
records.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve is motor only (general somatic motor).
records.clinical_testing: Tested with the other gaze nerves by having the patient track the tip of a pen through the visual field, watching for conjugate movement; failure of the superior oblique to act in conjugation with the other eye produces diplopia.
records.note: Links the BodyParts3D 4.0 inventory records named in geometry_record_ids, which carry geometry in the nervous system module (Milestone 9).

records.name: Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
records.root_values: Arises from the pons.
records.course: From the pons, the nerve divides into three divisions that leave the cranium separately: the ophthalmic division through the superior orbital fissure, the maxillary division through the foramen rotundum, and the mandibular division through the foramen ovale.
records.motor_distribution: The muscles of mastication (special visceral motor, via the mandibular division).
records.sensory_distribution: General sensation (GSS) from the face and head, by division — ophthalmic: scalp, forehead and nose; maxillary: cheeks, lower eyelid, nasal mucosa, upper lip, upper teeth and palate; mandibular: anterior two-thirds of the tongue (general sensation), skin over the mandible and lower teeth.
records.clinical_testing: Sensory function is tested by discrimination on the face: while the patient's eyes are closed, the examiner alternates the cotton tip (light touch) and the snapped pointed end (pain) of a cotton-tipped applicator, and the patient identifies whether the stimulus is sharp or dull. The nerve is also the sensory component of the jaw-jerk reflex, via its mesencephalic nucleus, which processes proprioceptive information of the face.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Abducens nerve (CN VI)
records.root_values: Arises at the pontine–medulla junction of the brainstem.
records.course: From the pontine–medulla junction, the nerve passes to the orbit and enters it through the superior orbital fissure.
records.motor_distribution: The lateral rectus muscle (general somatic motor), which abducts the eye.
records.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve is motor only (general somatic motor).
records.clinical_testing: Tested by having the patient track the tip of a pen through the visual field: in horizontal gaze the lateral rectus of one eye acts with the medial rectus of the other. Failure of one eye to abduct while the other adducts is internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and diplopia results from any failure of the extraocular muscles to move one eye in perfect conjugation with the other.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Facial nerve (CN VII)
records.root_values: Arises at the pontine–medulla junction of the brainstem.
records.course: From the pontine–medulla junction, the nerve enters the internal acoustic meatus and ultimately leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.
records.motor_distribution: The muscles of facial expression (special visceral motor). Visceral motor (GVM, parasympathetic): the lacrimal gland, the submandibular and sublingual glands, and the mucous glands of the mouth and nose.
records.sensory_distribution: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and from the hard and soft palates (special visceral sensory); general sensation from part of the external ear (GSS).
records.clinical_testing: Taste is tested by introducing salty, sour, bitter or sweet stimuli to either side of the tongue. The muscles of facial expression are tested by directed contraction against resistance — for example, the patient squeezes her eyes shut while the examiner tries to pry them open; the muscles of the upper and lower face both need to be tested, and severe deficits are obvious as one side of the face not moving like the other.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)
records.root_values: Arises at the pontine–medulla junction; its vestibular and cochlear divisions carry equilibrium and auditory sensations from the inner ear to the medulla.
records.course: The two divisions emerge from the inner ear, pass through the internal auditory (acoustic) meatus, and synapse in nuclei of the superior medulla.
records.motor_distribution: None — the nerve is purely sensory (special somatic sensory, SSS).
records.sensory_distribution: Hearing (cochlear division) and balance / equilibrium (vestibular division) (special somatic sensory).
records.clinical_testing: Hearing is tested with a tuning fork: in the Rinne test the vibrating fork is placed on the mastoid process until the sound is no longer heard, then moved beside the ear canal — if the sound is then not heard, a conductive hearing deficit is present; in the Weber test the fork is placed on top of the skull, and with unilateral conductive loss the sound is louder in the affected ear, while with unilateral sensorineural loss it is quieter in that ear. Equilibrium is assessed through the vestibulo-ocular reflex. Ménière's disease can affect both systems, with vertigo, a low-frequency ringing in the ears, or a loss of hearing.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
records.root_values: Arises from the medulla oblongata, posterior to the olive.
records.course: From the medulla, the nerve leaves the cranium through the jugular foramen.
records.motor_distribution: The stylopharyngeus muscle (special visceral motor). Visceral motor (GVM, parasympathetic): the parotid gland, via fibres that synapse in the otic ganglion.
records.sensory_distribution: Taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue (SVS); general sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue, part of the external ear and the middle ear cavity (GSS); visceral sensation from the carotid body and carotid sinus (GVS).
records.clinical_testing: The nerve relays general sensation from the pharyngeal walls and forms the afferent limb of the gag reflex: moving a tongue depressor to contact the lateral wall of the fauces should elicit the gag reflex, and stimulation of either side should elicit an equivalent response. Taste from the posterior tongue is tested with salty, sour, bitter or sweet stimuli applied to the tongue.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Vagus nerve (CN X)
records.root_values: Arises from the medulla oblongata, posterior to the olive.
records.course: From the medulla, the nerve leaves the cranium through the jugular foramen and descends through the neck; it has autonomic functions in the thoracic and superior abdominal cavities.
records.motor_distribution: Most muscles of the pharynx and larynx (special visceral motor) — the vagus directly stimulates the contraction of skeletal muscles in the pharynx and larynx to contribute to the swallowing and speech functions; smooth muscle of the pharynx, larynx and most of the gastrointestinal tract (general visceral motor).
records.sensory_distribution: Visceral sensation from the larynx, pharynx and the thoracic and abdominal viscera (GVS); general sensation from part of the external ear, the larynx and the pharynx (GSS); taste from the epiglottis region of the tongue (SVS).
records.clinical_testing: Motor function is tested through the gag reflex — the motor response, contraction of the muscles of the pharynx, is mediated through the vagus nerve — and by having the patient repeat consonant sounds such as 'lah-kah-pah' while the examiner observes the movements of the soft palate and the arches between the palate and the tongue.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Accessory nerve (CN XI)
records.root_values: Cranial root from the medulla (nucleus ambiguus); spinal root from the upper cervical spinal cord.
records.course: The spinal root ascends and enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum; the nerve then exits the skull through the jugular foramen to reach the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
records.motor_distribution: The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles (general somatic motor); a few fibres run with the vagus nerve to the viscera (special visceral motor).
records.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve is motor only.
records.clinical_testing: Tested by asking the patient to shrug both shoulders against resistance (trapezius) and to flex and extend the neck, or laterally flex the neck toward the shoulder, against resistance (sternocleidomastoid and trapezius); any difference on one side versus the other would suggest damage on the weaker side.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33). ta_name/ta_code follow the linked FMA records' Milestone 35 outcome (TA2 6356, nervus accessorius spinalis); the Milestone 9 whole-nerve clinical record (nerve.cn-11-accessory) carries the Milestone 23 outcome TA2 6352, nervus accessorius.

records.name: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
records.root_values: Arises from the medulla oblongata, anterior to the olive.
records.course: From the medulla, the nerve leaves the cranium through the hypoglossal canal and passes to the tongue.
records.motor_distribution: The intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (general somatic motor), except the palatoglossus, which is controlled by the vagus nerve.
records.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve is motor only (general somatic motor).
records.clinical_testing: Tested by asking the patient to stick out the tongue: the genioglossus is responsible for protrusion, so if the nerve on one side has a deficit, the tongue sticks out toward the side with the damage. Loss of function of the tongue can interfere with speech and swallowing.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Superior trunk of brachial plexus
records.root_values: Formed by the union of the anterior rami of C5 and C6; the roots emerge between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
records.course: The trunk traverses the posterior triangle of the neck and divides into anterior and posterior divisions, which go on to form the cords of the plexus.
records.motor_distribution: Gives off the suprascapular nerve (to supraspinatus and infraspinatus) and the nerve to subclavius; its fibres continue via the lateral and posterior cords into the terminal nerves of the upper limb.
records.sensory_distribution: Carries the C5–C6 sensory fibres of the upper limb; upper trunk injury produces sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the upper limb.
records.clinical_testing: Upper trunk (C5–C6) injury is Erb's palsy: the suprascapular, axillary and musculocutaneous nerves are predominantly affected, with loss of abduction and lateral rotation of the arm, loss of supination and loss of shoulder flexion, sensory loss on the lateral aspect of the upper limb, and the characteristic 'waiter's tip' position of the limb.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Middle trunk of brachial plexus
records.root_values: Formed by the anterior ramus of C7 alone.
records.course: The trunk traverses the posterior triangle of the neck and divides into anterior and posterior divisions, which go on to form the cords of the plexus.
records.motor_distribution: Motor fibres of C7 pass through the trunk into the lateral cord (via the anterior division) and the posterior cord (via the posterior division), and so into the terminal nerves of the upper limb; the plexus account lists no branches arising from the middle trunk itself.
verify: sensory_distribution: no sensory distribution specific to the middle trunk is stated in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
clinical_testing: no lesion pattern or bedside test specific to the middle trunk is described in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Inferior trunk of brachial plexus
records.root_values: Formed by the union of the anterior rami of C8 and T1; the roots emerge between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
records.course: The trunk traverses the posterior triangle of the neck and divides into anterior and posterior divisions; the anterior division continues as the medial cord of the plexus.
records.motor_distribution: Its fibres reach the hand via the medial cord and the ulnar and median nerves, which supply the intrinsic muscles of the hand.
records.sensory_distribution: Carries the C8–T1 sensory fibres of the upper limb; lower trunk injury produces sensory loss along the medial side of the upper limb.
records.clinical_testing: Lower trunk (C8–T1) injury is Klumpke's palsy: the ulnar and median nerves are predominantly affected, the intrinsic muscles of the hand are affected with sensory loss on the medial side of the upper limb, and the hand is left clawed.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Lateral cord of brachial plexus
records.root_values: Formed by the union of the anterior divisions of the superior and middle trunks; root values C5, C6 and C7. The cords of the plexus are named by their relationship to the axillary artery.
records.course: Lies lateral to the axillary artery in the axilla; gives off the lateral pectoral nerve, then divides into the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.
records.motor_distribution: Motor fibres pass into the musculocutaneous nerve (coracobrachialis, biceps brachii and brachialis) and, via the lateral root of the median nerve, into the median nerve's muscles of the forearm and hand.
records.sensory_distribution: Sensory fibres pass into the musculocutaneous nerve, continuing as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (lateral forearm), and into the median nerve (lateral palm and the palmar surface of the lateral three and a half digits).
verify: clinical_testing: no lesion pattern or bedside test specific to the lateral cord is described in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Posterior cord of brachial plexus
records.root_values: Formed by the union of the posterior divisions of all three trunks; root values C5–T1. The cords of the plexus are named by their relationship to the axillary artery.
records.course: Lies posterior to the axillary artery in the axilla; gives off the subscapular nerves and the thoracodorsal nerve, then divides into the axillary nerve and the radial nerve.
records.motor_distribution: Motor fibres pass into the axillary nerve (deltoid and teres minor) and the radial nerve (triceps brachii, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and the posterior compartment of the forearm).
records.sensory_distribution: Sensory fibres pass into the axillary nerve (skin over the inferior part of the deltoid) and the radial nerve's cutaneous branches (posterior arm, posterior forearm, lower lateral arm, and the dorsal surface of the lateral hand and digits).
verify: clinical_testing: no lesion pattern or bedside test specific to the posterior cord is described in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Medial cord of brachial plexus
records.root_values: Formed by the anterior division of the inferior trunk; root values C8 and T1. The cords of the plexus are named by their relationship to the axillary artery.
records.course: Lies medial to the axillary artery in the axilla; gives off the medial pectoral nerve, the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm, then divides into the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve.
records.motor_distribution: Motor fibres pass into the ulnar nerve (flexor carpi ulnaris, the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus and the intrinsic muscles of the hand) and, via the medial root of the median nerve, into the median nerve's muscles.
records.sensory_distribution: Gives off the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm (medial arm) and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm (medial forearm) directly; further sensory fibres continue into the ulnar nerve (medial palm, and the medial one and a half digits).
verify: clinical_testing: no lesion pattern or bedside test specific to the medial cord is described in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Suprascapular nerve
records.root_values: Arises from the superior trunk of the brachial plexus; root values C5 and C6.
records.course: Passes through the suprascapular notch, inferior to the superior transverse scapular ligament, to reach the posterior scapular region.
records.motor_distribution: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
records.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve has no cutaneous branches.
verify: clinical_testing: no bedside test or lesion pattern specific to the suprascapular nerve is stated in the consulted sources; not entered - verify
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Long thoracic nerve
records.root_values: Arises from the roots of the brachial plexus; root values C5, C6 and C7 (ventral primary rami).
records.course: Descends on the superficial surface of the serratus anterior muscle.
records.motor_distribution: Serratus anterior.
records.sensory_distribution: None — the nerve has no cutaneous branches.
records.clinical_testing: Lesion of the nerve causes winging of the scapula (scapular winging), through paralysis of its muscle, the serratus anterior.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Musculocutaneous nerve
records.root_values: Terminal branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus; root values C5, C6 and C7.
records.course: Arises in the axilla, pierces the coracobrachialis, then descends between the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles, and continues beyond the elbow as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
records.motor_distribution: Coracobrachialis, biceps brachii and brachialis — the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm.
records.sensory_distribution: Continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, supplying the skin of the lateral side of the forearm.
records.clinical_testing: Injury to the nerve weakens flexion of the elbow and of the shoulder, and weakens supination of the forearm, with sensory loss over the lateral forearm.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Axillary nerve
records.root_values: Terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; root values C5 and C6.
records.course: Arises in the axilla, exits the axilla through the quadrangular space, and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus to reach the deltoid.
records.motor_distribution: Deltoid and teres minor.
records.sensory_distribution: Via its branch, the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm: the skin over the inferior part of the deltoid — the 'regimental badge' area.
records.clinical_testing: Most commonly injured by fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or by shoulder dislocation: the deltoid is paralysed, so the arm cannot be abducted beyond the initial 15 degrees (the range supplied by supraspinatus), with sensory loss over the regimental badge area. Named bedside tests in the source include the deltoid extension lag sign and the external rotation lag sign.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Radial nerve
records.root_values: Terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; root values C5–T1.
records.course: Arises in the axilla, leaves via the triangular interval into the posterior compartment of the arm, descends in the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus, crosses anterior to the lateral epicondyle at the elbow, and divides into a deep branch — which passes through the supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve — and a superficial sensory branch.
records.motor_distribution: Triceps brachii, brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus, and — via the deep / posterior interosseous branch — the extensor muscles of the posterior compartment of the forearm.
records.sensory_distribution: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm, the lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm; and, via the superficial branch, the dorsal surface of the lateral three and a half digits.
records.clinical_testing: Lesion in the axilla: paralysis of the triceps as well as of the wrist extensors, giving wrist drop. Lesion in the radial groove: wrist drop, but the triceps is weakened rather than paralysed (its branches arise proximal to the groove). Lesion of the deep branch alone: no wrist drop (extensor carpi radialis longus is spared) and no sensory loss.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Median nerve
records.root_values: Formed in the axilla by the lateral and medial roots, from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus; root values C6–T1, with C5 fibres present in some people.
records.course: Descends through the arm, first lateral and then medial to the brachial artery; passes through the cubital fossa, between the two heads of pronator teres, and deep to flexor digitorum superficialis in the forearm; enters the hand through the carpal tunnel and divides into the recurrent branch and the palmar digital branches.
records.motor_distribution: In the forearm: pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor digitorum superficialis; via the anterior interosseous branch: flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus. In the hand: the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals.
records.sensory_distribution: The palmar cutaneous branch supplies the lateral part of the palm; the palmar digital branches supply the palmar surface of the lateral three and a half digits.
records.clinical_testing: Carpal tunnel syndrome is assessed with Tinel's sign and Phalen's manoeuvre; the palmar cutaneous branch is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome, because it does not pass through the carpal tunnel. A lesion at the elbow produces the 'hand of benediction' on attempted finger flexion, a supinated forearm and thenar wasting; a lesion at the wrist affects only the hand, the forearm muscles being spared.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Ulnar nerve
records.root_values: Continuation of the medial cord of the brachial plexus; root values C8 and T1.
records.course: Arises in the axilla and descends the medial side of the arm; at mid-arm it penetrates the medial intermuscular septum into the posterior compartment, passes behind the elbow through the ulnar tunnel (between the medial epicondyle and the olecranon), pierces the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, and runs deep to that muscle in the forearm; at the wrist it passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum and enters the hand through the ulnar (Guyon's) canal, dividing into superficial and deep branches.
records.motor_distribution: In the forearm: flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus. In the hand, via the deep branch: the hypothenar muscles, the medial two lumbricals, adductor pollicis and the palmar and dorsal interossei; palmaris brevis via the superficial branch. Together, all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals.
records.sensory_distribution: The palmar cutaneous branch supplies the medial half of the palm; the dorsal cutaneous branch supplies the dorsal surface of the medial one and a half fingers and the associated dorsal hand; the superficial branch supplies the palmar surface of the medial one and a half fingers.
records.clinical_testing: Froment's sign: the patient holds a piece of paper between thumb and index finger while the examiner pulls it away; if the adductor pollicis is paralysed, the thumb's interphalangeal joint flexes to hold the paper — a positive sign. Lesion at the elbow (for example medial epicondyle trauma or cubital tunnel compression): all ulnar muscles are affected, wrist flexion occurs with abduction, finger abduction and adduction are lost, Froment's sign is positive, all sensory branches are lost and the hypothenar eminence wastes. Lesion at the wrist: only the intrinsic hand muscles are affected, and the dorsal cutaneous branch is spared, so sensory loss is confined to the palmar medial one and a half fingers.
records.note: Links the sided FMA 5.1.0 concept records named in geometry_record_ids; those records are geometry-absent — the FMA is an ontology and carries no mesh data (Milestone 33).

records.name: Medial cutaneous nerve of arm
records.root_values: Branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus (root values C8 and T1 via the cord).
records.course: Arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus; communicates with the intercostobrachial nerve.
records.motor_distribution: None — a cutaneous (sensory) nerve.
records.sensory_distribution: Skin of the medial side of the arm.

records.name: Femoral nerve
records.root_values: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus, formed from the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4.
records.course: Travels inferiorly through the substance of psoas major, passes under the inguinal ligament into the femoral triangle, lateral to the femoral vessels and outside the femoral sheath, and about 4 cm below the inguinal ligament divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
records.motor_distribution: Hip flexors: pectineus, iliacus and sartorius. Knee extensors: the quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius).
records.sensory_distribution: The anterior cutaneous branches supply the anteromedial thigh; the saphenous nerve, its terminal branch, supplies the medial side of the leg and foot.
records.clinical_testing: In a lumbar plexopathy affecting the femoral nerve: weakness of hip flexion, impaired knee extension, and a reduced patellar reflex.

records.name: Obturator nerve
records.root_values: Formed from the anterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4 (lumbar plexus).
records.course: Descends through the fibres of psoas major and emerges from its medial border, travels along the lateral pelvic wall to the obturator foramen, and enters the medial compartment of the thigh through the obturator canal, dividing into anterior and posterior divisions that pass in front of and behind adductor brevis.
records.motor_distribution: The muscles of the medial compartment of the thigh — adductor longus, adductor brevis, the adductor part of adductor magnus, gracilis and obturator externus — the hip adductors, excepting the hamstring part of adductor magnus.
records.sensory_distribution: Via its cutaneous branch: the skin of the middle part of the medial thigh.
records.clinical_testing: The nerve can be damaged during pelvic or abdominal surgery, causing numbness and paraesthesia on the medial side of the thigh, weakness of thigh adduction, and problems with posture and gait arising from the loss of adduction.

records.name: Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh
records.root_values: Branch of the lumbar plexus; root values L2 and L3.
records.course: Arises from the lumbar plexus and enters the thigh at the lateral aspect of the inguinal ligament.
records.motor_distribution: None — the nerve is purely sensory.
records.sensory_distribution: The skin of the anterior and lateral aspects of the thigh, down to the knee.
records.clinical_testing: In a lumbar plexopathy, involvement of this nerve produces sensory loss over the lateral thigh.

records.name: Saphenous nerve
records.root_values: Terminal branch of the femoral nerve, arising from its posterior division (root values L2–L4 via the femoral nerve).
records.course: Travels through the adductor (subsartorial) canal with the femoral vessels, and exits the canal before the adductor hiatus to reach the medial side of the leg.
records.motor_distribution: None — the saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous (sensory) branch of the femoral nerve.
records.sensory_distribution: The medial side of the leg and foot.
records.clinical_testing: The nerve accompanies the long (great) saphenous vein in the leg and can be damaged during stripping of that vein, causing pain, paraesthesia or complete sensory loss on the medial side of the lower leg.

records.name: Sciatic nerve
records.root_values: From the sacral plexus; root values L4–S3. The largest nerve in the body, about 2 cm wide as a flat band; it consists of two nerves — the tibial and common fibular nerves — bound together in a single connective tissue sheath.
records.course: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, emerging inferior to the piriformis; descends, crossing the posterior surfaces of the superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus and quadratus femoris; enters the posterior compartment of the thigh deep to the long head of biceps femoris; and bifurcates at the apex of the popliteal fossa into the tibial and common fibular nerves (in about 12% of people the two divisions separate as they leave the pelvis).
records.motor_distribution: Directly: the posterior compartment of the thigh (biceps femoris, semimembranosus and semitendinosus) and the hamstring portion of adductor magnus. Indirectly, via its terminal branches: all the muscles of the leg and foot. The nerve innervates no muscles in the gluteal region.
records.sensory_distribution: No direct sensory functions; indirectly, via its terminal branches, it supplies the lateral leg, the heel, and the dorsal and plantar surfaces of the foot.
records.clinical_testing: Piriformis syndrome — compression of the nerve by the piriformis muscle — presents with radicular pain, numbness and muscle weakness and buttock tenderness, and the pain may be exacerbated by internal rotation of the lower limb at the hip. Injection safety: the nerve passes through the lower medial quadrant of the gluteal region, so intramuscular injections are made only into the upper lateral quadrant.

records.name: Tibial nerve
records.root_values: Terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; root values L4–S3.
records.course: Arises at the apex of the popliteal fossa, travels through the fossa and descends in the posterior compartment of the leg, passes posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel (beneath the flexor retinaculum), and terminates just distal to the tunnel by dividing into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.
records.motor_distribution: The posterior compartment of the leg — superficial: plantaris, soleus and gastrocnemius; deep: popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus and tibialis posterior. In the foot, via the medial and lateral plantar branches: the intrinsic muscles of the sole, except extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis (deep fibular nerve).
records.sensory_distribution: Via the branches that contribute to the sural nerve: the posterolateral leg and the lateral foot. The medial calcaneal branches supply the heel. The medial plantar branch supplies the plantar surface of the medial three and a half digits and the associated sole; the lateral plantar branch the lateral one and a half digits and the associated sole — together, the whole sole of the foot.
records.clinical_testing: Tarsal tunnel syndrome — entrapment of the nerve in the tarsal tunnel — causes altered sensation in the sole of the foot and, in severe cases, weakness and wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the foot. Damage to the nerve causes loss of plantarflexion and loss of flexion of the toes, and weakened inversion of the foot.

records.name: Common fibular (peroneal) nerve
records.root_values: Terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; root values L4–S2.
records.course: Arises at the apex of the popliteal fossa where the sciatic nerve bifurcates, follows the medial border of biceps femoris inferolaterally across the lateral head of gastrocnemius, wraps around the neck of the fibula between the attachments of fibularis longus, and divides into the superficial fibular and deep fibular nerves.
records.motor_distribution: Directly: the short head of biceps femoris. Via the superficial fibular nerve: the lateral compartment of the leg (fibularis longus and brevis — eversion). Via the deep fibular nerve: the anterior compartment of the leg (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus — dorsiflexion and extension of the digits) and some intrinsic muscles of the foot.
records.sensory_distribution: The lateral sural cutaneous branch supplies the upper lateral leg; the sural communicating branch joins the tibial contribution to form the sural nerve (lower posterolateral leg). Via the superficial fibular nerve: the anterolateral leg and the dorsum of the foot except the first web space. Via the deep fibular nerve: the first web space.
records.clinical_testing: The nerve is most commonly damaged at the neck of the fibula, by fracture or by a tight plaster cast: dorsiflexion is lost and the foot is held in plantarflexion — footdrop, with its characteristic gait; eversion and extension of the digits are also lost, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral leg, while the medial leg (saphenous territory) and the heel and sole (tibial territory) are preserved.

records.name: Superficial fibular nerve
records.root_values: Terminal division of the common fibular nerve (root values L4–S2 via the common fibular nerve).
records.course: Arises where the common fibular nerve divides at the neck of the fibula, and descends within the lateral compartment of the leg.
records.motor_distribution: Fibularis (peroneus) longus and fibularis brevis — eversion of the foot.
records.sensory_distribution: The anterolateral leg and the dorsum of the foot, except the first web space (deep fibular nerve).
records.clinical_testing: Its function is lost in the parent nerve's lesion at the fibular neck: eversion is lost, together with the dorsiflexion supplied by the deep fibular division, in footdrop.

records.name: Deep fibular nerve
records.root_values: Terminal division of the common fibular nerve (root values L4–S2 via the common fibular nerve).
records.course: Arises where the common fibular nerve divides at the neck of the fibula, and descends within the anterior compartment of the leg.
records.motor_distribution: The anterior compartment of the leg — tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius — and the muscles on the dorsum of the foot, extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis.
records.sensory_distribution: The web space between the great toe and the second toe (the first web space).
records.clinical_testing: Anterior compartment syndrome of the leg can damage the deep fibular nerve, resulting in foot drop; a deep fibular palsy can itself produce footdrop.

records.name: Sural nerve
records.root_values: Formed by the union of the medial sural cutaneous nerve (a branch of the tibial nerve) with the fibular communicating branch of the lateral sural cutaneous nerve (from the common fibular nerve); it has no spinal root values of its own.
records.course: Formed in the leg by the union of the medial sural cutaneous nerve with the fibular communicating branch, and descends in the posterior leg.
records.motor_distribution: None — a cutaneous nerve, formed from sensory branches of the tibial and common fibular nerves.
records.sensory_distribution: The posterior surface of the leg and the lateral side of the foot.

records.name: Pudendal nerve
records.root_values: Formed on the posterior pelvic wall from the anterior divisions of the ventral rami of S2, S3 and S4 (sacral plexus).
records.course: Descends between the piriformis and ischiococcygeus muscles, leaves the pelvis through the lower part of the greater sciatic foramen, crosses the sacrospinous ligament near the ischial spine, re-enters the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen, and runs with the internal pudendal artery and vein through the pudendal (Alcock's) canal in the fascia over obturator internus, dividing into the inferior rectal nerve, the perineal nerve and the dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris.
records.motor_distribution: Via the perineal nerve: bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, levator ani and the external urethral sphincter; via the inferior rectal nerve: the external anal sphincter — together, the somatic control of urinary and faecal continence.
records.sensory_distribution: The external genitalia of both sexes and the skin of the perineum: the perianal skin and the lower third of the anal canal (inferior rectal nerve); the perineum and the labia majora and minora, or the posterior scrotum (perineal nerve); and the skin of the penis or clitoris (dorsal nerve).
records.clinical_testing: Clinical procedure — the pudendal nerve block, used to provide analgesia for vaginal childbirth, episiotomy repair and minor vaginal procedures: with the patient in the lithotomy position, the ischial spine is palpated transvaginally and local anaesthetic is injected around the spine, aspirating before injecting because the internal pudendal artery accompanies the nerve.
